edits.old: International Water, a subsidiary of Bechtel with United Utilities, held 55% of Aguas del Tunari, the only bidder for the Cochabamba concession; Abengoa of Spain held 25% (Wikipedia).
edits.new: The ICSID tribunal's decision on jurisdiction of 21 October 2005 sets out the ownership as at September 1999 (para. 60): International Water (Tunari) Ltd of the Cayman Islands held 55% of Aguas del Tunari and was itself 100% owned by Bechtel Enterprise Holding, Inc. of the United States; Riverstar International S.A. of Uruguay, 100% owned by Abengoa of Spain, held 25%; and four Bolivian companies held 5% each - Constructora Petricevic S.A., Compania Boliviana de Ingenieria S.R.L., ICE Agua y Energia S.A. and Sociedad Boliviana de Cemento S.A. Under an agreement of 9 November 1999 Edison S.p.A. of Italy was to take a 50% interest in International Water (Tunari) Ltd (para. 67). The decision does not mention United Utilities. On 21 December 1999 IW Ltd migrated from the Cayman Islands to Luxembourg, becoming International Water (Tunari) S.a.r.l., and on 22 December a Dutch company, International Water (Tunari) B.V., became its sole shareholder, which is how the Netherlands-Bolivia treaty came into it; Bolivia calls the Dutch entities mere shells (paras 70, 72).

edits.old: China Eximbank and Bank of China signed a syndicated loan with Barisal Electric Power Company Ltd for the US$557.89 million plant in September 2021, according to AidData's current record. Energy Transition Bangladesh, citing AidData's 2023 record, says China Eximbank and the Beijing and Singapore branches of Bank of China signed a US$427.5 million loan in April 2020;
edits.new: AidData's record for the project, read on 11 November 2026, gives one syndicated loan facility of US$427.5 million signed in April 2020 (commitment date 1 April 2020) by China Eximbank with the Beijing and Singapore branches of Bank of China Limited, to Barisal Electric Power Company Ltd; AidData divides it equally at US$142.5 million each and says that split warrants further investigation. The US$557.89 million is the cost of the whole independent power plant project, not the loan. An earlier version of this card dated the signing to September 2021 and read the April 2020 loan as a separate one; both came from the same record.

edits.old: Global Energy Monitor reports that the syndicate issued its first loan in May 2021, completing the financing.
edits.new: Global Energy Monitor's Barisal power station page reports that the syndicate of China Eximbank and Bank of China issued the first loan in May 2021, citing a 12 May 2021 report, and describes the financing as closed at that point; it names the borrower as Barisal Power Generation Co., Ltd. where AidData names BEPCL. AidData's record gives no disbursement date. With the facility signed in April 2020 and the sovereign guarantee given on 23 December 2020, a first issuance in May 2021 does not conflict with the signing date, though no source says so in terms.
for a coal plant the operator, PT TJK Power, describes as 2 x 65 MW, that is 130 MW installed;

edits.old: The Jakarta Post gave the plant's share as 30% of Batam's 383 MW demand; Kompas gave 26%.
edits.new: The Jakarta Post gave the plant's share as 30% of Batam's 383 MW demand; Kompas gave 26%. The sources do not agree on capacity. PT TJK Power's own site gives the plant as 2 x 65 MW, 130 MW, which is the figure AidData uses. Teras Batam, reporting an online press conference on 4 November 2021, quotes PT Bright PLN Batam's president director Nyoman S Astawa saying the plant has operated since 2012 "dengan daya mampu sebesar 2 x 55 Mega Watt" - with an available capacity of 2 x 55 MW - and the same article describes the plant as running on "mesin pembangkit 55 MW x 2", two 55 MW generating sets. Daya mampu normally means the output a plant can actually deliver rather than its nameplate rating, which would make the two figures compatible, but neither source says so and the article's own wording treats 55 MW as the units' rating. TJK Power is a joint venture of PT Petra Unggul Sejahtera and PT PLN Batam, Petra Unggul Sejahtera being a partnership of China Huadian Engineering Co. Ltd, PT Inta Daya Perkasa and Batam Power Ventures Pte Ltd; its site dates the two units' commercial operation to 25 October and 1 November 2012. The Jakarta Post's 383 MW demand figure is 384 MW in Teras Batam, with the same 30 per cent share.

edits.old: The Bank says its role was only supervisory work under a contract that ended before the oil palm investment.
edits.new: The Bank says its role was only supervisory work under a contract that ended before the oil palm investment. IFAD's own evaluation gives the financing of the first phase as a US$20 million IFAD loan of April 1997 with private and government cofinancing, names no World Bank or IDA money, with further cofinancing of US$3.1 million from the beneficiaries, and records the Bank as the project's cooperating institution only until August 2004, with UNOPS taking over in September 2004; the evaluation says the Bank "was concerned about compliance with its internal environmental safeguards policies and felt unable to continue as cooperating institution". On the evaluation's account the Bank's role did not end before the oil palm investment: implementation of the oil palm subproject began in July 2003, and the Bank pushed for a revised environmental impact assessment and led the technical review and mid-term review missions before it left. A search of the World Bank projects API for Uganda with oil palm, Kalangala or vegetable oil returns nothing. The case still carries a World Bank lender key, which is under review.

edits.old: US$52 million loan to the Vegetable Oil Development Project; total cost US$146.2 million (The Ecologist).
edits.new: The Ecologist's US$52 million is the second phase, not the 1997 loan. IFAD's President's report of April 2010 (EB-2010-99-R-19) proposes an IFAD loan of SDR 33.5 million, about US$52 million, for Vegetable Oil Development Project Phase 2, against a total project cost of US$147.23 million, cofinanced by Oil Palm Uganda Limited (US$70.38 million), the Kalangala Oil Palm Growers Trust (US$5.48 million), the borrower (US$14.14 million), the beneficiaries (US$3.90 million), an SNV grant and an IFAD grant. Phase one, approved by IFAD's Executive Board in April 1997, was a US$20 million IFAD loan against an original total cost of US$60 million.
